title: Deeper installment: explode the items without losing the order
goal: Turn one parent array into child rows while preserving parent identity and choosing null-preserving behavior deliberately.
tag: Certification cycle 5 · focused lesson 2 · nested transformation
concept:
A packing slip has one order number and several item lines. If you cut off the item lines without copying the order number onto each one, the pieces become useless.

An explode or flatten operation turns each array element into a row. That changes cardinality: one parent can become many rows. An outer form can also keep a parent whose array is null by emitting one row with a null child.
example: Order O-10 has items A and B. Order O-11 has a null items field. A normal explode yields two rows, both for O-10. An outer explode yields those same two rows plus O-11, NULL. The extra row is useful only if “an order with no readable items” must remain visible for diagnosis or a later left-side count.

use_case.when: Use array expansion when downstream work needs one row per nested child while retaining the parent key.
use_case.example: A bronze order event contains an items array; silver needs one order-item row for SKU-level revenue and a visible exception for an order with no item array.
use_case.decision: Use ordinary expansion when null parents should disappear. Use outer expansion when parent preservation is part of the contract. Measure input parents, output children, and null-child rows so fan-out does not silently inflate aggregates.

practice: Choose normal or outer behavior and inspect exactly which order-item rows survive. Predict the parent count and output count first.
boundary: The local model expands two fixed arrays. It does not parse VARIANT values, distinguish missing from JSON null, recurse through multiple arrays, model skew, shuffle cost, malformed children, permissions, warehouse size, or vendor execution.

Predict first. Which FLATTEN column carries the child value? VALUE. Keep the source alias beside it.

title: An unbounded executor queue can make maximumPoolSize irrelevant
goal: Predict whether a Java ThreadPoolExecutor creates a thread, queues work, or rejects it from its core size and queue policy.
tag: Java concurrency foundation · Java SE 26 checked
concept:
A restaurant has two cooks, space for an unlimited stack of tickets, and a sign saying “up to eight cooks.” The manager never hires cook three because the ticket stack is never full.

ThreadPoolExecutor adds threads beyond corePoolSize only when the work queue cannot accept the task. An unbounded queue always accepts it, so the pool stays at the core size and maximumPoolSize does not help with the backlog.
example: Core size is 2, maximum size is 8, and ten slow requests arrive together. With an unbounded queue, two run and eight wait. With a bounded queue of two, two run, two queue, and later submissions can create up to six more workers before rejection policy applies.

use_case.when: Use this reasoning when a Java service shows rising queue delay even though maximumPoolSize looks generous.
use_case.example: A Kafka enrichment service has core=2, max=8, and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue; lag rises while the pool never exceeds two workers.
use_case.decision: Choose an unbounded queue only when smoothed bursts cannot outrun service capacity for long. Use a bounded queue, explicit rejection/backpressure, and load tests when latency and memory need hard limits.

practice: Switch the queue between unbounded and capacity two, then increase submitted work. Watch the same max-pool setting lead to different worker and queue counts.
boundary: The model assumes all tasks arrive before any finish and one task per worker. It omits task duration variance, keep-alive, prestarting, priorities, memory use, rejection handlers, shutdown, interrupts, virtual threads, and actual scheduling.

Two; the other eight queue

The unbounded queue accepts work after the two core workers are busy.
Why can a bounded queue grow the pool beyond core?

It changes Java syntax

steps.code: int core = 2; int max = 8; int submitted = 10; boolean unbounded = true;
steps.note: Configure the teaching pool and simultaneous burst.

steps.code: int running = Math.min(core, submitted); int remaining = submitted - running;
steps.note: The first two tasks occupy core workers.

steps.code: int queued = unbounded ? remaining : Math.min(2, remaining); boolean queueFull = !unbounded && queued == 2;
steps.note: The unbounded queue accepts every remaining task and never reports full.

steps.code: int extraWorkers = queueFull ? Math.min(max - core, remaining - queued) : 0; running += extraWorkers; String result = running + " running, " + queued + " queued";
steps.note: No full-queue signal means no non-core workers are created.

title: Scaling lead time spends headroom before new capacity arrives
goal: Set an autoscaling trigger early enough that demand growth does not exhaust the current fleet during detection and startup delay.
tag: Distinguished Engineer judgment · capacity and reliability
concept:
A fire engine called at the moment a building is fully on fire is already late. Autoscaling also has delay: metrics travel, a policy decides, resources start, and health checks pass.

Headroom is unused capacity held for that interval. A useful trigger accounts for how much demand can grow before replacement capacity becomes ready, plus uncertainty. A 90% target may be too late even when average utilization looks comfortable.
example: A service can handle 1,000 requests per second. It is receiving 750, growing by 70 per minute, and new nodes take four minutes to serve traffic. Before they arrive, demand reaches 1,030. To survive that deterministic ramp, the trigger must fire by 720 requests per second or earlier, before adding uncertainty.

use_case.when: Use lead-time headroom when capacity arrives minutes after demand changes and exhaustion causes queues, throttling, or SLO breaches.
use_case.example: An EKS API tier needs four minutes for metric propagation, node provisioning, image pull, and readiness while a partner launch adds 70 requests per second each minute.
use_case.decision: Use predictive or scheduled scaling for known events, target tracking with measured headroom for organic growth, and load shedding for bursts faster than any provisioning path. Re-measure lead time and growth instead of copying a universal percentage.

practice: Change growth and ready time. Watch the demand ramp cross the current capacity line and see the latest safe trigger move left.
boundary: This is a deterministic linear-growth model. It omits stochastic bursts, correlated failures, warm pools, nonlinear service curves, queueing, downstream bottlenecks, metric lag distributions, cost, and multi-region failover.

title: Return a durable task handle when a tool call will outlive the connection
goal: Use the MCP Tasks extension for long work while respecting polling, durable IDs, input requests, and cooperative cancellation.
tag: GenAI harness engineering · MCP Tasks extension 2026-07-28
concept:
A coat-check ticket is not the coat. It is a durable handle that lets you leave, return, and retrieve the result later.

The MCP Tasks extension lets a server return resultType: task from a supported tool call. The client persists the task ID and polls tasks/get at the suggested interval. The task may need input, complete, fail, or be cooperatively cancelled.
example: A deployment tool returns task T-42 with status working and a five-second poll interval. Later it becomes input_required for production approval. The client answers through tasks/update, resumes polling, and eventually receives the original tool result. A reconnect is safe because the task ID was stored durably.

use_case.when: Use a task handle when tool work can take minutes, cross a disconnect, wait for approval, or map onto an external durable job.
use_case.example: An agent starts an ECS deployment, disconnects, then resumes status checks and supplies an approval response without restarting the deployment.
use_case.decision: Keep ordinary tool results for short work. Use Tasks only after capability negotiation, persist opaque task IDs securely, honor pollIntervalMs, and design cancellation as intent rather than proof of termination.

practice: Advance T-42 through working, input required, resumed, and completed. Try cancellation and observe that acknowledgement does not force the terminal state.
boundary: This model is a fixed state machine. It does not run MCP, authenticate callers, encrypt task IDs, persist a server database, route HTTP headers, rate-limit polls, execute deployments, or prove cancellation.

title: Grow the infrared detector directly on the read-out chip
goal: Understand how monolithic in-situ PbS growth removes a bonding boundary while keeping the reported research limits visible.
concept:
A conventional infrared camera can be like placing a finished tile on top of a circuit and connecting every pixel through a separate bonding step. Misalignment, cost, and interface complexity grow with the array.

The reported method grows lead sulfide detector material directly on a CMOS read-out integrated circuit using a room-temperature aqueous process. The researchers controlled Pb–OH complexation and environmental disturbance to form quasi-single-crystalline films with pixel-level uniformity.
example: The paper reports a 640×512 array: 327,680 pixels. Its antimony-doped photodiodes reached specific detectivity of 4.4×1011 Jones at 2.5 µm and captured infrared images. Those are paper results for a demonstrated platform, not a guarantee of manufacturing yield or field reliability.

use_case.when: Use this research when evaluating lower-complexity integration of infrared detector material with read-out electronics, including flexible substrates.
use_case.example: A sensor team wants a high-resolution infrared focal-plane array without separately fabricating and bonding a detector wafer onto the ROIC.
use_case.decision: Treat monolithic aqueous growth as promising research evidence. Product adoption still needs independent data on yield, pixel defects, long-term stability, packaging, toxicity controls, calibration, environmental robustness, and process compatibility.

practice: Switch between bonded and in-situ integration. Watch the detector/read-out boundary change, then calculate the exact pixel count for the reported array.
boundary: The visual is a structural comparison, not a fabrication simulator. It does not model crystal growth, transport, detectivity, noise, defects, spectral response, toxicity, encapsulation, yield, or commercial cost.

title: Blue/green rollback switches traffic; it does not rewind shared data
goal: Separate environment deployment, traffic routing, health gates, and data compatibility in a GitHub Actions blue/green release.
concept:
A restaurant opens a fully prepared second dining room before sending guests there. If service fails, the host sends new guests back to the old room.

Blue/green deployment keeps the old version (blue) serving while the replacement (green) is installed and tested. A router shifts traffic only after checks. GitHub Actions can orchestrate jobs and protected environments; the actual traffic shift belongs to the deployment platform.
example: Blue serves 100% of checkout traffic. GitHub deploys green, smoke tests it, then CodeDeploy shifts 10% to green. If green errors, routing returns to blue. Any database writes green already made remain and must be backward-compatible or explicitly compensated.

use_case.when: Use blue/green when you need production-like validation and a fast traffic rollback while briefly paying for two environments.
use_case.example: An ECS checkout service deploys a new task set, receives a 10% canary, and returns traffic to the old task set if the error gate fails.
use_case.decision: Choose blue/green when routing is controllable and both versions can safely share dependencies. Prefer in-place for low-risk stateless work; use expand/contract schemas or isolated data paths when shared-data compatibility is not guaranteed.

practice: Move traffic from blue to green and inject a green failure. Observe routing reverse while the shared-data marker stays changed.
boundary: This model omits real GitHub jobs, AWS credentials, CodeDeploy configuration, health-check windows, DNS, sticky sessions, connection draining, queues, database migration details, cost, and region failure.

title: GraphQL serializes top-level mutation fields—not the whole distributed transaction
goal: Use mutation ordering correctly without mistaking serial resolver execution for atomicity or rollback.
concept:
A cashier handles “reserve item” before “charge card.” Doing those actions in order prevents them from starting together, but it does not erase the reservation if the charge fails.

The GraphQL specification executes the top-level fields of a mutation serially, in textual order. Other fields should be side-effect-free and may execute normally. Serial order is an execution rule, not a cross-service transaction.
example: A mutation calls reserveInventory and then chargeCard. Reservation succeeds; charging fails. The response can contain the reservation result and an error for charging. Inventory remains reserved unless the API explicitly releases it, makes the operation idempotent, or coordinates a durable workflow.

use_case.when: Use multiple top-level mutation fields when their textual order is meaningful and each field has a clear independently observable result.
use_case.example: An internal operations API reserves stock before attempting a payment, with an explicit release action on payment failure.
use_case.decision: Prefer one purpose-built mutation when the business operation needs one invariant and one idempotency key. Use serial top-level fields only when partial success is acceptable and compensation, retries, and authorization are designed explicitly.

practice: Fail the second mutation field and inspect what remains. Then switch to a single orchestrated field and compare the visible contract—not an assumed distributed transaction.
boundary: The model is sequential Python, not a GraphQL executor. It omits null propagation, aliases, fragments, transport retries, resolver concurrency below the top level, authorization, database transactions, federation, and actual compensation failure.

The second field fails after the reservation already exists.

steps.code: needs_compensation=reservation is not None and payment=='FAILED'; automatic_rollback=False
steps.note: The API must explicitly release or otherwise reconcile the reservation.

walkthrough.limit: The model is sequential Python, not a GraphQL executor. It omits null propagation, aliases, fragments, transport retries, resolver concurrency below the top level, authorization, database transactions, federation, and actual compensation failure.

sources: GraphQL Specification September 2025: executing the root selection set
Official GraphQL specification; published September 2025; checked November 5, 2026
visual_explanation: A two-step mutation timeline stops at the failed second field while the first field's effect remains visible, separating ordering from atomic rollback.
written_questions: Which existing mutation exposes multiple side effects that callers may wrongly assume are atomic?
Would one orchestrated mutation, a saga, or explicit compensation make its retry contract clearer?
